Energy materials & molecular science

Ankit Mathanker

Postdoctoral Scholar

University of Chicago / Argonne National Laboratory

Chicago, Illinois

I am a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Chicago / Argonne National Laboratory. My current research focuses on covalent organic frameworks as organic cathode materials for lithium-ion batteries, with the aim of improving capacity and stability.

I completed my Ph.D. in Chemical Engineering and Scientific Computing at the University of Michigan in August 2026. My doctoral work examined how electrode potential and electrolyte composition affect molecular adsorption and electrocatalytic reactions. I use density functional theory, molecular dynamics, and machine learning interatomic potentials to study these systems, and I also develop automated workflows for quantum chemistry.

Before Michigan, I studied the conversion of lignocellulosic biomass into biofuels at the University of Alberta. Across these projects, I am interested in connecting molecular-scale understanding with the design of materials and processes for energy applications.

Research

Materials, interfaces,
and chemical reactions

Current work · University of Chicago

Organic cathodes for lithium-ion batteries

Developing cathode materials based on covalent organic frameworks, with a focus on stable, high-capacity organic electrodes for lithium-ion batteries.

Doctoral research · University of Michigan

Electrochemical interfaces and catalysis

Studying how aqueous ions, electrode potential, and co-reactants influence adsorption and the hydrogenation of organic molecules. This work combines electronic-structure calculations, molecular dynamics, and comparisons with experiment.

Ion effects on adsorption

University of Michigan · Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory

Machine learning interatomic potentials

Developing and benchmarking interatomic potentials for metal–electrolyte interfaces. These models make it possible to sample interfacial water and ions over longer times while retaining a connection to first-principles calculations.

Potential-dependent interfacial properties

Ongoing collaboration

Automated quantum chemistry

Developing TSAgent, an agentic workflow for transition-state searches at the density functional theory level. The workflow plans calculations, evaluates their results, and revises the search as it proceeds.

Read the TSAgent preprint
